paper_title: Investor's Last Exam: Can AI Agents Do Equity Investment Without Seeing the Future?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Financial agents must form forecasts and investment judgments from decision-time evidence, with predictions evaluated against subsequent outcomes. Existing benchmarks assess financial knowledge, research workflows, or forecasting, but evaluating the full research process requires a strictly frozen information set and professional evaluation criteria. We introduce Investor's Last Exam (ILE), an equity-research benchmark led by experienced buy-side investors and fund managers. Its three components are a versioned financial database spanning 3.43 million document versions and nine source categories, supplemented by structured market data, with validated timestamps governing retrieval and computation; a task taxonomy organized around professional analyst deliverables; and an expert-led framework linking scoring criteria to sources, calculations, and assumptions through financial dependency graphs. Evaluation spans 86 assignments and jointly assesses research quality, forecast accuracy, and simulated investment performance. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 lead overall at 68.1 and 66.9 out of 100, yet even Astra scores only 52.5 on Forecast & Model. Our results show that even state-of-the-art models fail to translate overall research capability into predictive performance. ILE shifts the evaluation unit from isolated capabilities to the evidence--assumption--judgment chain, allowing researchers to locate where analytical advantages fail to translate into forecasts and investment judgments, and providing a traceable, diagnostic foundation for training and evaluating financial agents.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Buy-side equity research informs capital allocation decisions [4]. Researchers analyze companys operations, competitive position, and financial condition, model its future performance, and assess what these expectations imply for value, risk, and investment decisions. This process, from understanding business to forming an investment thesis, is central to professional equity analysis. However, question answering, retrieval, or isolated computational skills are insufficient to characterize AIs competence in this work [2, 16, 17]. Professional equity research is difficult to evaluate precisely because the quality of its judgments is not determined by any single capability, but by whether the analytical chain is coherent, the evidence is sufficient, and the forecasts withstand subsequent verification, attributes that are embedded in the real research process rather than capturable by isolated tasks. Existing financial benchmarks mostly cover isolated stages of the research workflow. FinanceBench [17] focuses on document QA, Finance Agent [2] and FinSearchComp [16] introduce agentic search, and FinBench [12] begins to evaluate forecasting and outcome validation. FinanceGym [34] further combines thesis-driven reports, expert-validated rubrics, and publication-date-filtered web corpus. However, publication-date filtering remains retrieval-level heuristic rather than system-level constraint. It provides only an approximate temporal boundary, and page metadata can be misaligned with content updates, so post-cutoff information may still enter retrieval, computation, and scoring. Consequently, none of these benchmarks enforces version-level availability across the full research pipeline, leaving look-ahead leakage and evidence provenance uncontrolled. What remains missing is an evaluation unit that connects evidence, assumptions, and conclusions under strict cutoff. To this end, we introduce Investors Last Exam (ILE), benchmark for professional investment research. It evaluates whether AI agents can work within realistic information boundary along the full analyst workflow, processing large-scale, interconnected financial data and documents to complete long-horizon tasks from evidence retrieval and assumption modeling to forecasting, valuation, and investment decisions. ILE has three components. First, versioned database of 3.43 million document versions across nine financial data categories (1.52 TB) that supports retrieval, computation, and evidence tracing within the pre-cutoff information set, upgrading the cutoff from retrieval-level date filtering to system-level constraint across data access, computation, and rubric review. Second, professional task taxonomy of five categories and twenty subtypes plus integrated assignments, which decomposes the analyst workflow into scorable professional judgments such as accounting reconciliation, assumption-sensitive forecasting, and evidence-based investment 2 Table 1 Design and evaluation features of financial benchmarks. Year denotes the first public release. Third, an expertAI pipeline that links scoring propositions to sources, calculations, and assumptions via financial dependency graphs, making reasoning paths for difficult tasks reviewable and traceable; experts provide questions and judgments, agents assemble retrievable and computable evidence, multiple models assist in review, and experts finalize the rubrics. Together, these components connect professional research to reviewable evidence and financial judgment, with expert criteria assessing both the analysis and designated outcomes to locate where agents succeed or fail. Table 1 summarizes how existing benchmarks differ along these dimensions. We conduct experiments on eleven systems. GPT-6 Astra leads overall at 68.1, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 at 66.9, but Astra scores 78.9 on Research & Evidence and 77.6 on Evaluate & Decide while earning only 52.5 on Forecast & Model, indicating that evidence organization and investment judgment are comparatively mature, whereas forecast construction remains clear weakness. This weakness directly manifests as reordering under predictive criteria: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash leads realized forecast-outcome criteria, and Kimi K3 earns higher simulated returns than Opus despite lower research score. This indicates that supporting analysis, forecast outcomes, and investment performance do not share single ordering, and that an aggregate score alone cannot characterize research capability. We further trace score differences to specific financial dependencies and errors: systems reconcile cash-flow identities but struggle to separate operating improvement from temporary cash movements; they produce coherent driver bridges and recommendations but fail to ensure that assumptions, accounting states, and outputs form testable financial model; submission control and error recovery are additional failure sources; and expert refinement shows that some errors reflect ambiguous scoring requirements rather than model capability alone. Overall, failures concentrate in forecast assumptions, accounting scope, financial interpretation, and decision consistency rather than in retrieval or arithmetic, indicating that the bottleneck for financial agents has shifted from information access to assumption calibration and model consistency. Our main contributions are as follows: time-frozen research environment. Built on versioned corpus, it enforces source-version availability across retrieval and computation, so agents can access only pre-decision evidence and look-ahead leakage is suppressed at the mechanism level. An expert-constructed task suite and evaluation framework. Tasks are authored by buy-side experts, and each scored requirement is anchored to evidence, financial dependencies, and verifiable criteria, traceable to specific source document or calculation. multidimensional evaluation of forecasting and investment research. Spanning forecast formation, valuation judgment, and investment decisions, it links judgments to supporting analyses and realized outcomes, assessing both outcome accuracy and reasoning consistency. 3 Figure 3 Expert-led construction with AI-assisted search and review. Experts frame questions, build evidence-linked financial dependencies, and refine questions and rubrics. The refinancing graph illustrates covenant constraint on drawable credit. sections.title: 2 Benchmark Design
sections.content: The design goal of ILE is to evaluate equity research under strict information boundary: it uses professional research deliverables as task carriers and versioned evidence as the information boundary (Figure 2), so that the evidence available to the agent at decision time and the financial requirements its answer must satisfy are constrained together. Section 2.1 defines versioned evidence and the information cutoff, Section 2.2 presents the deliverable taxonomy and financial dependencies, and Section 2.3 details the expert-led construction framework that links scoring criteria to evidence, calculations, and assumptions.

sections.title: 2.1 Financial Research Environment
sections.content: Merely constraining the query by date does not guarantee that the retrieved results stay within the specified cutoff. In the Tesla task O74 shown in Figure 4 (left), GPT-6 Astra Codex trajectory issued query containing before:2026-03-24, yet retrieved source dated July 2 that reported realized Q2 deliveries. This is because pages publication date need not reflect when its content actually became available, and missing metadata, updated pages, and retrospective reports can all bypass date filtering [21]. Date filters constrain the query rather than the retrieved information, so page can retain an early publication date while carrying later content. To make the time constraint apply to the information itself, we build continuously updated corpus that retains every historical version and assigns each version an availability time. As of 15 October 2026, the corpus contains 3,430,336 document versions and 1.52 TB of material [26], and is continually expanded with new disclosures and revisions while earlier versions are never overwritten. Sources fall into nine categories, covering financial reports, structured statements, earnings calls, investor materials, issuer events, analyst estimates, research reports, institutional holdings, and news. Structured market data support price, return, and volatility analysis, and coverage spans the US, mainland Chinese, Hong Kong, and other markets (Appendix B). Each versions availability time is established at collection time rather than inferred afterwards. Every immutable 4 version records its publication or release time, timezone, and precision, together with supporting time evidence. Timestamp normalization uses conservative availability boundary. For records with unverified timestamps, we first employ state-of-the-art models to infer and cross-validate their publication dates and identify potential subsequent updates. Records are excluded from task access only when reliable availability time cannot be established, and each revision receives its own availability time. Once established, availability time must take effect across the toolchain the agent actually uses. Each task defines timezone-aware cutoff tc and authorized datasets; version is eligible only if its availability time precedes tc, regardless of its reporting period. The shared tool library enforces this boundary across the whole toolchain rather than at the search entry alone. Search, reads, downloads, and cached results share the same authorization and availability checks (Appendix B.2). search discovers eligible source versions and read returns their passages and tables. Structured-table tools query authorized records and freeze the results, so that later revisions cannot alter data already retrieved. download and table_download retrieve eligible source files and export frozen results, respectively, both writing to the task workspace, where bash supports file inspection, numerical analysis, and model building with network access disabled. Agents can therefore work autonomously with complete files and tables, leveraging subagent-assisted reading and context compression to build forecasts and reconciliations even when the required evidence exceeds the models context window, while keeping all inputs within the cutoff. Source and version references link calculations to eligible evidence, tool records make the analysis inspectable, and submit_answer validates the deliverable format. The evaluation side remains information-isolated, with reference analyses, rubrics, and later disclosures kept private from the agent. Forecast settlement then matches the target metric, period, and unit. Appendix I.5 evaluates the tool library on external financial tasks.

sections.title: 2.2 Professional Task Taxonomy
sections.content: The taxonomy derives from the research practice of experienced buy-side analysts and fund managers. That practice is organized around deliverables, spanning four stages: screening opportunities, building evidence and forecasts, making investment recommendations, and monitoring theses. The taxonomy is structured around these same deliverables. Tasks are classified by their principal analyst deliverable  (Table 2)  : five categories contain twenty subtypes, Integrated Research combines these functions into full report, and Market Trading captures the ultimate downstream objective of investment research, targeting realized prices, returns, or volatility. task has one category even when it involves several analytical operations, and Appendix gives the detailed professional judgments and subtype definitions. Financial difficulty in these tasks comes from the interdependence among measurements, assumptions, and decisions. Inputs must be comparable across reporting definitions; new evidence must justify the magnitude and scope of forecast update; and an investment stance must follow from the model and identify the evidence that would reverse it. Plausible facts and local calculations alone do not satisfy these requirements, which also explains why the taxonomy does not classify tasks by topic. Two cases illustrate how these dependencies surface. Microsoft O58 shows why reporting scope matters, since cloud revenue spans the three segments and cannot be added as fourth. AEP N27 tests whether higher operating cash flow implies lower financing needs once investment spending and cash-flow adjustments are considered. Section 4.1 traces the latter from question to evidence and criterion-level results, and Appendix gives additional cases.

sections.title: 2.3 Expert-Led Task Construction
sections.content: Building on the taxonomy, this section explains how tasks are constructed. Construction begins with experts fixing the task elements: drawing on their research practice, they specify the entity or universe, period, deliverable, and investment judgment (Figure 3), where the deliverable and investment judgment directly correspond to the classification basis of the previous section. These questions in turn drive data development; when required source classes are missing, acquisition, parsing, and version tracking are expanded, yielding reusable coverage under the same information boundary. The core of construction is to transform each task into verifiable financial dependency graph that connects source-grounded facts, financial assumptions, intermediate calculations, and investment judgments through 5 Figure 4 Information validity and financial interpretation. Left: in Tesla task O74, GPT-6 Astras public-web Codex search returns realized Q2 deliveries from post-cutoff source despite dated query. Right: higher AEP operating cash inflow coexists with wider pre-financing shortfall. AEP amounts are USD millions; investing use and construction denote outflows. Each AEP badge counts how many of the 11 evaluated systems earn full credit on every criterion in the indicated group of this tasks rubric, under GPT-6 Astra grading. explicit financial relationships. While building the reference analysis, experts use search and read to select source passages and attach them to claims and calculations; each fact retains its issuer, period, unit, source version, and location, and relations express the financial rules connecting inputs and outputs, such as an accounting identity, revenue bridge, or peer read-through. This is precisely how the interdependence among measurements, assumptions, and decisions described in the previous section materializes within an individual task. AI-assisted investigation then searches for missing evidence, tests assumptions, and proposes counterexamples, with multiple state-of-the-art models reviewing drafts, but whether suggestion is adopted is decided by the expert. The refinancing example illustrates this division of labor. Cash plus cash flow plus unused credit appears sufficient until borrowing covenant is examined, at which point the expert adds the decisive dependency, namely whether credit is drawable in that state, to the question, reference analysis, and rubric. Once construction is complete, each scoring criterion is linked to supporting evidence, reproducible calculation, or an explicit financial judgment, making the evaluation traceable and verifiable. Experts then review cutoff validity, units, accounting scope, assumptions, and questionrubric alignment, while the rubric specifies weights, evidence, and tolerances or partial credit. Trial answers expose ambiguity and incomplete financial arguments, and authors trace discrepancies to the affected source, assumption, question, or scoring rule and revise that component. Expert review ultimately determines whether the scoring rules test the intended financial judgment, including the validity of accounting definitions, forecast assumptions, and reward incentives. AWS O15 offers an instance of calibration. sections.title: 3.1 Protocol and scoring
sections.content: This section describes how the evaluation runs, how answers are scored in terms of criteria and formula, how the two evaluation modes apply, and how results are reported. All models in the main evaluation share single tool library, organized into six families: search, read, download, table_operations, bash, and submit_answer. Each task allows 7,200 seconds and up to three submissions, using the same public inputs and cutoff-eligible data [26]; prompts and tool schemas are given in Appendix J. Answers are scored against common standard. All tasks use weighted criteria on common 0100 scale, and the rubric dimensions describe the requirements assessed within an answer: requested outputs (Result), source support and measurement basis (Evidence), economic interpretation (Financial logic), numerical operations (Calculation), consistency among linked quantities (Reconciliation), alignment of conclusions with the analysis and mandate (Decision consistency), and risks and sensitivity (Uncertainty). Definitions and examples are given in Appendix E.1. Scoring is carried out by two kinds of judges: numerical criteria are scored by 7 deterministic checks, and semantic criteria are judged by GPT-6 Astra. Model-based evaluation can exhibit position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases [37]; Appendix I.3 reports sensitivity to the choice of judge. Market tasks instead use single 100-point Result criterion, computed from the declared price or ranking loss. sections.title: 3.2 Performance across financial tasks
sections.content: Strong financial analysis does not necessarily translate into accurate forecasts. We examine whether models that excel at evidence-based research and financial reasoning also perform well on forward-looking prediction tasks. Astra leads overall at 68.1, followed by Opus at 66.9  (Table 3)  , yet their profiles of strength differ: Opus leads Result and Calculation, while Astra leads Financial logic, Reconciliation, Decision consistency, and Uncertainty, and Qwen Max leads Evidence (Table 3a). The difference concentrates in forecasting. Astra scores 78.9 on Research & Evidence and 77.6 on Evaluate & Decide, but only 52.5 on Forecast & Model and 66.3 on Integrated Research, with KPI and cross-company forecasting at 41.1 and 49.6. Opus leads Forecast & Model (52.6) and Monitor & Update (64.2). These scores jointly point to persistent weakness in estimating future drivers and peer effects. When predictive performance is taken as the yardstick, the ranking changes: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash leads at 40.3, ahead of Astra at 37.7 and Opus at 37.6, and DeepSeek V4 Pro leads the Market Trading category at 64.6 despite an overall score of 59.3 (Appendix G.1). Overall research quality and predictive performance therefore capture different strengths. Beyond final scores, the demanding multi-step research workflows in ILE reveal substantial differences in models tool-use patterns and agentic capabilities. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash averages 73.8 interaction rounds and 113.8 tool calls per task, making the most retrieval and computation calls, while the overall leader Astra makes fewer; Kimi K3 averages 26.7 rounds and DeepSeek V4 Pro 34.1, both above the 10.4 and 21.3 reported by FrontierFinance [36], and Finance Agent Benchmark reports 13.5 rounds for o3 [2] (Appendix I.1). Opus and Qwen Max have similar read and computation counts yet differ by 4.8 points. On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash scores 63.0 at USD 0.36 per task, whereas Opus gains 3.9 points at USD 7.96, roughly 22 times the cost (Figure 5). These results highlight the agentic demands of financial research, where effective performance requires not merely extensive tool use, but the ability to coordinate evidence retrieval, computation, and financial reasoning across multi-step workflows. 8 Figure 5 Score, cost, and tool use. sections.title: 3.3 From fundamental forecasts to stock returns
sections.content: To test whether forecasts translate into realized returns, we construct trades on retrospective sample of twenty assignments covering eleven companies and thirteen disclosures. Forecasts above or below archived pre-cutoff analyst estimates generate long or short signals, while conflicting votes and missing forecasts hold cash. Capital is allocated equally across opportunities; entry is the first close after the cutoff and exit is the first trading-day close after disclosure, with costs of 10 basis points per leg plus 3% annualized short borrowing. Hunyuan leads this sample at 8.50%, followed by Flash at 7.98% and Astra at 7.18%, versus 1.18% for always long. Kimis 7.15% exceeds Opuss 6.39% despite its lower research score. Returns depend on forecast coverage, direction relative to expectations, and the subsequent stock move; the capability measured by research scores and the capability reflected in trading returns do not coincide, and the former does not guarantee the latter (Appendix I.2). sections.title: 3.4 Public-web research and database coverage
sections.content: Further, we hold the shared task set, scoring standard, and cutoff fixed and vary only the evidence source, in order to examine whether comparable scores imply comparable compliance. Astra scores 68.1 on our database and 68.3 on public-web Codex, while Qwen Max and Hunyuan score higher on our database (Appendix I.4). Comparable scores, however, do not imply comparable boundary: 57% of Astras public-web trajectories contain post-cutoff sources, including the target quarters realized Microsoft revenue and Tesla deliveries, despite dated query (Figure 4). These trajectories draw on evidence available only after the cutoff, and their scores cannot be regarded as obtained within the information boundary. Comparable scores therefore establish comparable answer quality only; whether the evidence precedes the cutoff cannot be read off the score and is guaranteed only by the evidence source itself.

sections.title: 4 Where Financial Research Breaks Down
sections.content: Our case analyses reveal three recurring challenges in financial research: tracing cash flows to funding needs while distinguishing sustainable improvements from temporary movements, evaluating the predictive validity of financial assumptions, and ensuring that assumptions and outputs form consistent financial model. We illustrate these challenges through representative tasks, then examine submission reliability and the role of expert rubric refinement.

sections.title: 4.1 A complete case: from cash flows to a funding judgment
sections.content: Question, dependency, and cash-flow quality. AEP N27 asks how funding needs and fuel-cost recovery changed between the first halves of 2025 and 2026. Its report must connect disclosed cash flows to external financing needs and explain the quality of the change (Figure 4, right). The first breakdown lies in the dependency itself. Operating cash flow rises from USD 2,671 million to 3,421 million, while investing cash use rises from 5,347 million to 6,602 million; the pre-financing shortfall, investing use less operating inflow, therefore widens from 2,676 million to 3,181 million, an increase of 505 million. Construction spending grows by 1,586 million, exceeding the 1,255 million increase in net investing use because other investment items partly offset it. The second breakdown lies in explaining cash-flow quality. Net income falls by 441 million and non-cash adjustments rise by 516 million, together explaining only 75 million of the 750 million operating-cash improvement, with the remainder coming mainly from other noncurrent-liability movements that contribute 540 million, driven by customer deposits and rate-rider refund timing. The net deferred-fuel adjustment improves by 72 million but does not identify gross fuel collections. Without this distinction, operating improvement is easily misread as sustainable cash generation. What separates systems. The eleven evaluated systems all recover the eight reported inputs and reconcile both cash-flow identities, yet only five compute both funding shortfalls, three distinguish net fuel adjustments from gross collections, and five reach the supported funding conclusion. Recovering inputs and completing calculations therefore does not amount to understanding the dependencies; an answer must separate operating improvement from temporary cash movements and combine that assessment with capital needs. Appendix H.4 gives the full decomposition.

sections.title: 4.2 Calculation, forecasting, and joint consistency
sections.content: Predictive validity cannot be established by arithmetic. In Tesla O80, three systems earn every supportinganalysis point but no forecast-outcome credit. Their units, revenue bridges, and recommendations are coherent, yet deliveries, revenue, and margin all miss their realized targets. Historical observations can support several plausible assumptions about future demand, pricing, and cost, and arithmetic propagates whichever assumptions are chosen without establishing their predictive validity (Appendix G). Assumptions and outputs must satisfy jointly testable consistency constraints. At the accounting level, Home BancShares N41 requires expense, payment, and payable forecasts to describe single accounting state, and any forecast that departs from that state fails. At the level of argument, GE Aerospace N06 requires position limit to follow from supported equity-downside assumption; Qwen Max earns full formula credit yet offers no explanation of its protection boundary, showing that correct formula does not amount to valid argument. Disclosed obligations, accounting reserves, and equity losses measure different quantities, and combining them into downside estimate requires an explicit financial argument. Both kinds of tasks test whether assumptions and outputs form valid financial model (Appendix H.5).

sections.title: 4.3 Submission Reliability and Task Completion
sections.content: Submission failures reveal distinct limitation of financial research agents: producing useful analysis does not guarantee successful completion of the required deliverable. Hunyuan stops without submitting on 17 trajectories, and Opus has three rejected submissions on each of five. Such failures prevent answer quality from translating into task completion, and Table 5 quantifies this gap, with full strict results in Appendix E.3.

sections.title: 4.4 What expert refinement improves
sections.content: If scoring criteria remain at the level of general financial requirements, errors cannot be traced to specific step and therefore cannot be attributed. Expert review serves to break such requirements into distinguishable criteria, so that each kind of error has corresponding test. Microsoft O58 separates additive reporting segments from overlapping Cloud revenue, making double counting testable scope error. JPMorgan O26 fixes dated prior before peer disclosures, so that an update must be attributable to new evidence rather than an unstated baseline. sections.title: 5 Limitations
sections.content: Although ILE restricts look-ahead bias during retrieval through its versioned database, frontier models may already have implicitly memorized some historical outcomes during pre-training [13]; fully disentangling internal knowledge from external retrieval will require counterfactual or cold-start experiments. In addition, some ILE tasks are settled against realized disclosures or market prices, and correct intermediate reasoning does not guarantee an accurate forecast: exogenous market noise can lead otherwise sound analyses to numerically deviate from realized values, so evaluating agents solely on outcome accuracy would underestimate research quality. In future work, we will pursue two directions. First, we will build counterfactual and synthetic financialscenario engine that perturbs real financial statements and constructs virtual peer companies, forcing agents to reason solely from retrieved evidence and thereby isolating parametric memory at its source. Second, we will restructure tasks and evaluation: decomposing long expert-authored assignments into composable micro-task graphs, combined with difficulty-weighted scoring and multi-model consensus judging protocol; and for forecast-type tasks, we will also refine the evaluation to better distinguish reasoning failures from stochastic fluctuations, advancing ILE toward living benchmark that can expand continuously with new market disclosures.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduce Investors Last Exam (ILE), benchmark for professional equity research that combines versioned financial database, professional task taxonomy, and an expert-led construction framework. ILE enforces decision-time information boundaries across retrieval and computation over 3.43 million document versions, while financial dependency graphs link scoring criteria to source evidence, calculations, and assumptions. Experiments on eleven systems show that strong supporting analysis does not consistently translate into accurate forecasts and well-supported financial conclusions: GPT-6 Astra leads overall at 68.1, but scores 52.5 on Forecast & Model. Forecast-outcome scores and simulated investment returns further produce different model rankings. Dependency-level analysis locates errors in driver assumptions, accounting scope, and the financial interpretation of calculated quantities. By making the evidenceassumptionjudgment chain the unit of evaluation, ILE connects research quality to realized outcomes and provides traceable, diagnostic foundation for measuring and improving financial agents ability to turn evidence into reliable forecasts and defensible investment decisions.

sections.title: A Related Work
sections.content: Financial questions and research workflows. FinQA evaluates numerical reasoning over financial documents [7]; TAT-QA combines tables and associated text [39], and ConvFinQA extends numerical reasoning to conversational chains [8]. FinBen broadens evaluation across financial tasks, including forecasting and decisionmaking [35]. FinanceBench pairs open-book questions with answers and evidence [17]. Finance Agent Benchmark and its v2 extension evaluate expert-authored analyst assignments with retrieval tools [2, 30]. FinSearchComp studies professional financial search and reasoning [16]; DeepResearch Bench evaluates longer research reports and citations beyond finance [9]. ILE organizes tasks by their financial deliverable and couples research with task-specific information boundary. Professional deliverables and expert rubrics. GDPval evaluates expert-created work products across occupations [25]. APEX-Agents extends professional evaluation to long-horizon, cross-application workflows, including investment banking [31]; BankerToolBench evaluates end-to-end investment-banking workflows through financial models, presentations, and reports graded against expert-defined criteria [22]. These benchmarks motivate evaluation through professional deliverables. ILE focuses on buy-side equity research under version-level information cutoffs and additionally evaluates designated forecasts against realized outcomes. Beyond finance, PaperBench uses expert-developed hierarchical rubrics for research replication [28], while LLM-Rubric studies multidimensional evaluation and calibration [15]. RubricBench documents gap between human-authored and model-generated criteria [38], motivating explicit validation of the criteria themselves. Evidence-linked assessment. BigFinanceBench uses weighted rubrics for derivation steps [32]; Samayas FrontierFinance uses expert-authored, source-attributed rubrics across investor workflows [36]. The distinct FrontierFinance benchmark from Krumdick et al. emphasizes long-horizon computer-use financial modeling and includes human evaluation [20]. Classical data-provenance research distinguishes source locations from the input dependencies that explain an output [3]. ALCE evaluates citation-supported generation [11], and VeriScore assesses verifiable claims in long-form responses [27]. ILEs financial dependency graph connects the proposition being graded to the calculation, assumption, and source version that support it. Experts can inspect and edit these dependencies while allowing solvers to develop their own analytical route. Forecasting and historical information environments. ForecastBench evaluates future-event forecasts [18]; Bench to the Future supplies an offline pastcasting corpus [10]. FinDeepForecast constructs live financial forecasts over timestamped database [23], and FinBench focuses on time-gated calibration [12]. Agentic Time Machine approximates historical web access [5]. FinanceHarness/FinanceGym combines self-collected, publicationdated web corpus with point-in-time search, an entity graph for task generation, expert validation, and pre-/post-cutoff criteria [34]. ILE integrates versioned financial data, professional equity-research deliverables, and an expert-authored dependency-level construction workflow. Samayas FrontierFinance instead uses dated queries and applies retrieval cutoff to its in-house index while excluding predictive queries [36]. StockBench measures trading-agent performance [6]. Research on data vintages and look-ahead bias examines how temporal data access and pretrained knowledge affect forecasting evaluations [1, 13, 19, 21, 24, 29]. LiveBench reduces contamination risk through regularly refreshed questions and objective scoring [33].

C.1 Financial dependencies across assignments Comparable measurements must be reconstructed before they can be modeled. Tesla task O70 asks for annual automotive revenue over FY20162025, its sales, regulatory-credit, and leasing components, and bridge from income-statement to segment presentation. The solver must identify changes in reporting definitions and document their effect on comparability. Home BancShares task N41 requires forecasts of interest expense, cash interest paid, and closing interest payable that obey one accounting identity. These tasks assess whether individually plausible numbers form valid financial representation. New evidence must justify specific change in forecast. JPMorgan task O26 requires dated prior, capitalmarkets peer signal, and an explicit coefficient translating that signal into investment-banking fees and Markets 17 revenue. Unaffected lines must retain their prior values, and the changes must reconcile to the updated totals. AWS task O15 similarly requires an itemized forecast-revision bridge and reasons for leaving other drivers unchanged. The required judgment is the magnitude and scope of the update supported by each disclosure. An investment decision must remain consistent with its assumptions and reversal conditions. Apple task O09 combines an earnings forecast with an investment stance and material risks. JPMorgan task O32 asks which earnings drivers are durable and which developments would change the stance. GE Aerospace task N06 requires loss-constrained equity weight supported by an explicit downside assumption, while distinguishing supported obligations, accounting reserves, and guarantee exposure. These assignments test whether the agent can turn financial analysis into decision whose assumptions and conditions can be examined.

sections.title: D A Worked Financial Dependency
sections.content: JPMorgan task O26 asks how capital-markets peer disclosure changes previously formed forecast. The solver first fixes Q2 2026 prior using information available by March 31, 2026, 16:00 ET, then incorporates peer signal available by the tasks May 14 cutoff. Let I0 and M0 denote prior investment-banking fees and Markets revenue, gI and gM the peers disclosed growth rates, and β the chosen read-through coefficient. The affected-line updates are = βgI I0, = βgM M0, (2) with updated totals obtained by adding these increments to the prior and holding other lines fixed. The source and period of each peer signal, the dated prior, the choice of β, and the reconciliation to CIB and total revenue are distinct verification targets. For example, Astras revised answer uses I0 = 2,714.04, gI = 0.12, and β = 0.5, producing = 162.8424 million. The equation makes arithmetic reproducible; source evidence and the coefficients justification establish whether the update is financially supported.

sections.title: E Rubric Dimensions and Score Aggregation
sections.content: E.1 Dimension definitions Rubric dimensions classify the financial requirement evaluated by an individual criterion. Each criterion carries one dimension label, while an assignment can contain criteria from several dimensions. Professional task categories instead identify the assignments principal deliverable (Appendix C). Table 9 defines the dimensions using examples from the benchmarks rubrics. The distinction between Evidence, Calculation, and Reconciliation follows the object being checked. In O01, the Evidence criteria establish whether growth inputs use the required reporting basis and fiscal period. In N27, the Calculation criteria derive funding shortfall from disclosed cash flows, while Reconciliation criteria check cash-flow and cash-balance identities across linked figures. Financial logic evaluates the interpretation of these relationships; Decision consistency evaluates whether the resulting conclusion follows from the analysis.
